name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Element in liquid state for high temperature measurement

questiontext.text: The element which exists in liquid state for a wide range of temperature and can be used for measuring high temperature is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An element used in high-temperature thermometry must have a relatively low melting point to remain molten near room temperature and an exceptionally high boiling point to stay in the liquid phase over a wide temperature interval without vaporizing.

Step 2: Property Evaluation
Among the Group 13 elements, gallium has an unusually low melting point of approximately \(303\text{ K}\) (\(30\text{ }^\circ\text{C}\)) due to its unique crystal structure consisting of discrete \(\mathrm{Ga}_2\) pairs, yet it has a very high boiling point of about \(2513\text{ K}\) (\(2240\text{ }^\circ\text{C}\)). This gives gallium a remarkably wide liquid range of over \(2200\text{ }^\circ\text{C}\), making it ideal for measuring high temperatures.

Step 3: Comparison with Other Elements
Boron has a very high melting point and is a hard solid at ambient temperatures. Aluminium and indium do not possess the same combination of low melting point and extremely broad liquid range as gallium.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The element that exists in the liquid state over a wide range of temperature and is used in high-temperature thermometry is gallium (\(\mathrm{Ga}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - Identification of Lewis acid among metal chlorides

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a Lewis acid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A Lewis acid is defined as a chemical species capable of accepting an electron pair due to the presence of an incomplete valence shell (an electron-deficient center) or accessible vacant orbitals.

Step 2: Electronic Configuration and Valence Octet
In monomeric aluminium chloride, \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\), the central aluminium atom is bonded to three chlorine atoms via single covalent bonds, sharing a total of six valence electrons. Because aluminium has an incomplete octet, it readily accepts an electron pair from a donor base to achieve a stable octet configuration, thus acting as a classical Lewis acid.

Step 3: Nature of Alkaline Earth Metal Chlorides
Magnesium chloride (\(\mathrm{MgCl}_2\)), calcium chloride (\(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\)), and barium chloride (\(\mathrm{BaCl}_2\)) are predominantly ionic compounds comprising divalent cations and chloride anions, each possessing stable, filled noble-gas valence shells, and do not act as electron-pair acceptors in this context.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The species that acts as a Lewis acid is aluminium chloride (\(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - Hybridisation and geometry of tetrahydroxido complex species

questiontext.text: The geometry of a complex species can be understood from the knowledge of type of hybridisation of orbitals of central atom. The hybridisation of orbitals of central atom in \(\left[\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{OH})_{4}\right]^{-}\) and the geometry of the complex are respectively

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The steric number of the central atom in a coordination entity equals the number of \(\sigma\) bonds plus lone pairs on the central atom. A steric number of 4 with zero lone pairs corresponds to \(sp^3\) hybridisation and a tetrahedral geometry.

Step 2: Bonding and Hybridisation Analysis
In a four-coordinate hydroxido complex of a second-period element with four single \(\sigma\) bonds to \(\mathrm{OH}^{-}\) ligands, the central atom utilizes one \(s\) and three \(p\) valence orbitals to form four equivalent hybrid orbitals directed toward the four corners of a regular tetrahedron.

Step 3: Geometry Deduction
With four bonding electron pairs and no unshared valence electron pairs on the central atom, repulsion between the electron pairs is minimized when they adopt tetrahedral bond angles of \(109.5^\circ\). Therefore, the hybridisation is \(sp^3\) and the geometry is tetrahedral.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The hybridisation and geometry of the complex species are \(sp^3\) and tetrahedral, respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - Acidic nature of Group thirteen element oxides

questiontext.text: Which of the following oxides is acidic in nature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Across Group 13 from top to bottom, metallic character increases as atomic size increases and ionisation enthalpy generally decreases. Consequently, the nature of their oxides changes from acidic to amphoteric and finally to basic.

Step 2: Analysis of Group 13 Oxides
Boron is a non-metal with high electronegativity; its oxide, \(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{O}_3\), is acidic and reacts with basic oxides to form metal borates, or with water to form boric acid. Aluminium oxide (\(\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) and gallium oxide (\(\mathrm{Ga}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) are amphoteric, whereas indium oxide (\(\mathrm{In}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)) and thallium oxide are predominantly basic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The oxide that is acidic in nature is diboron trioxide (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q05 - Coordination number limitation due to vacant orbitals

questiontext.text: The exhibition of highest co-ordination number depends on the availability of vacant orbitals in the central atom. Which of the following elements is not likely to act as central atom in \(\mathrm{MF}_6^{3-}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The maximum coordination number of an element is determined by the total number of valence shell orbitals available for bonding. Expansion of the coordination number beyond 4 requires energetically accessible vacant \(d\)-orbitals.

Step 2: Orbital Availability in Group 13 Elements
Boron belongs to the second period of the periodic table with an electronic configuration of \(1s^2\, 2s^2\, 2p^1\). In the second principal shell (\(n = 2\)), only one \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals exist; there are no \(2d\) orbitals. Hence, boron can accommodate at most 8 electrons in four orbitals, restricting its maximum covalency and coordination number to 4.

Step 3: Behavior of Heavier Congeners
Heavier Group 13 elements such as aluminium, gallium, and indium have accessible vacant \(d\)-orbitals in their valence shells, allowing them to expand their octets and form six-coordinate octahedral complex anions such as \(\left[\mathrm{AlF}_6\right]^{3-}\), \(\left[\mathrm{GaF}_6\right]^{3-}\), and \(\left[\mathrm{InF}_6\right]^{3-}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Due to the absence of vacant \(d\)-orbitals, boron cannot act as the central atom in \(\mathrm{MF}_6^{3-}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q06 - Mechanism of acidic behavior of boric acid

questiontext.text: Boric acid is an acid because its molecule

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Orthoboric acid, \(\mathrm{B(OH)}_3\) or \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{BO}_3\), is not a protic acid (it does not donate protons directly from its own molecule). Instead, it behaves as a weak monobasic Lewis acid.

Step 2: Reaction in Aqueous Solution
Boron has an incomplete octet with only six valence electrons in planar \(\mathrm{B(OH)}_3\). In aqueous solution, it accepts a pair of electrons from the lone pair of an oxygen atom of a water molecule (effectively accepting a hydroxyl ion, \(\mathrm{OH}^{-}\)), completing its octet to form the tetrahedral \(\left[\mathrm{B(OH)}_4\right]^{-}\) anion and releasing a hydronium ion (proton):
\[\mathrm{B(OH)}_3 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \left[\mathrm{B(OH)}_4\right]^{-} + \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^{+}\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Boric acid acts as an acid because it accepts \(\mathrm{OH}^{-}\) from water, releasing a proton into the solution.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q07 - Catenation tendency order in group fourteen elements

questiontext.text: Catenation i.e., linking of similar atoms depends on size and electronic configuration of atoms. The tendency of catenation in Group 14 elements follows the order:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Catenation is the ability of an element to form self-linking covalent bonds creating chains and rings. It depends primarily on the strength of the element–element single bond (\(\mathrm{M}-\mathrm{M}\) bond enthalpy) and atomic size.

Step 2: Evaluation of Bond Enthalpies
As atomic radius increases down Group 14, orbital overlap becomes progressively more diffuse and weaker. The bond enthalpies are approximately: \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C} \approx 348\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{Si}-\mathrm{Si} \approx 297\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{Ge}-\mathrm{Ge} \approx 260\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\), and \(\mathrm{Sn}-\mathrm{Sn} \approx 240\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\). Because \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}\) bonds are exceptionally strong, carbon shows an overwhelmingly superior tendency toward catenation compared to silicon, while germanium and tin show much smaller and comparable tendencies. Lead does not show catenation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of catenation tendency is \(\mathrm{C} \gg \mathrm{Si} > \mathrm{Ge} \approx \mathrm{Sn}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q08 - Controlling chain length in silicone polymer synthesis

questiontext.text: Silicon has a strong tendency to form polymers like silicones. The chain length of silicone polymer can be controlled by adding

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the manufacture of silicone polymers, the hydrolysis of methylchlorosilanes produces silanols, which then undergo condensation polymerisation. The number of chlorine atoms determines the functionality and connectivity of the silanol intermediate.

Step 2: Role of Monochlorosilane as Chain Terminator
Hydrolysis of dimethyldichlorosilane, \(\mathrm{Me}_2\mathrm{SiCl}_2\), produces dimethylsilanediol, \(\mathrm{Me}_2\mathrm{Si(OH)}_2\), which has two reactive \({-}\mathrm{OH}\) groups and propagates linear chains. In contrast, trimethylchlorosilane, \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\), has only one chlorine atom; upon hydrolysis, it yields trimethylsilanol, \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiOH}\), with a single reactive \({-}\mathrm{OH}\) group. When \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiOH}\) condenses onto a growing siloxane chain, it blocks the terminal site, preventing further addition of monomers and terminating chain growth.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The chain length of silicone polymers is controlled by adding trimethylchlorosilane (\(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q09 - Trend of first ionisation enthalpy in group thirteen

questiontext.text: Ionisation enthalpy (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\mathrm{H}_{1}\text{ kJ}\cdot\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\)) for the elements of Group 13 follows the order.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Down a group, first ionisation enthalpy generally decreases due to increased atomic size and increased shielding. However, in Group 13, anomalous variations occur due to the poor shielding of intervening \(3d\) and \(4f\) subshells.

Step 2: Analysis of the Group 13 Trend
- Moving from \(\mathrm{B}\) (\(801\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)) to \(\mathrm{Al}\) (\(577\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)), ionisation enthalpy decreases significantly as atomic size increases.
- Moving from \(\mathrm{Al}\) to \(\mathrm{Ga}\) (\(579\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)), the addition of ten intervening \(3d\)-electrons with poor shielding increases effective nuclear charge, causing ionisation enthalpy to rise slightly (\(\mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Ga}\)).
- Moving from \(\mathrm{Ga}\) to \(\mathrm{In}\) (\(558\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)), increased shielding by the larger core causes ionisation enthalpy to decrease (\(\mathrm{Ga} > \mathrm{In}\)).
- Moving from \(\mathrm{In}\) to \(\mathrm{Tl}\) (\(589\text{ kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1}\)), the presence of fourteen intervening \(4f\)-electrons with very poor shielding (lanthanoid contraction) markedly increases effective nuclear charge, causing ionisation enthalpy to rise again (\(\mathrm{In} < \mathrm{Tl}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of first ionisation enthalpy is \(\mathrm{B} > \mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Ga} > \mathrm{In} < \mathrm{Tl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q10 - Planar arrangement of atoms in diborane structure

questiontext.text: In the structure of diborane

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In diborane (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)), each boron atom undergoes \(sp^3\) hybridisation. The molecule consists of two terminal \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds on each boron atom and two three-centre two-electron (\(3c-2e\)) bridging \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{B}\) bonds.

Step 2: Spatial Orientation of Atoms
The two boron atoms and the four terminal hydrogen atoms lie in a single plane. The two bridging hydrogen atoms lie in a plane perpendicular to this plane, with one bridging hydrogen positioned above the plane and the other positioned below the plane.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The structure consists of 2 boron atoms and 4 terminal hydrogen atoms in the same plane, and 2 bridging hydrogen atoms lying in the perpendicular plane.

answer.text: All hydrogen atoms lie in one plane and boron atoms lie in a plane perpendicular to this plane.
2 boron atoms and 4 terminal hydrogen atoms lie in the same plane and 2 bridging hydrogen atoms lie in the perpendicular plane.
4 bridging hydrogen atoms and boron atoms lie in one plane and two terminal hydrogen atoms lie in a plane perpendicular to this plane.
All the atoms are in the same plane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q11 - Synthesis of diborane and inorganic benzene borazine

questiontext.text: A compound X, of boron reacts with \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) on heating to give another compound Y which is called inorganic benzene. The compound X can be prepared by treating \(\mathrm{BF}_3\) with Lithium aluminium hydride. The compounds X and Y are represented by the formulas.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of Compound X
Boron trifluoride (\(\mathrm{BF}_3\)) reacts with lithium aluminium hydride (\(\mathrm{LiAlH}_4\)) in diethyl ether to produce diborane (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)):
\[4\mathrm{BF}_3 + 3\mathrm{LiAlH}_4 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6 + 3\mathrm{LiF} + 3\mathrm{AlF}_3\]
Hence, compound X is \(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\).

Step 2: Identification of Compound Y
When diborane reacts with ammonia and the intermediate product is heated, it forms borazine, \(\mathrm{B}_3\mathrm{N}_3\mathrm{H}_6\), which is isoelectronic and isostructural with benzene and commonly termed inorganic benzene:
\[3\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6 + 6\mathrm{NH}_3 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{B}_3\mathrm{N}_3\mathrm{H}_6 + 12\mathrm{H}_2\]
Hence, compound Y is \(\mathrm{B}_3\mathrm{N}_3\mathrm{H}_6\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The formulas of compounds X and Y are \(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\) and \(\mathrm{B}_3\mathrm{N}_3\mathrm{H}_6\), respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q12 - Composition of piezoelectric quartz crystal material

questiontext.text: Quartz is extensively used as a piezoelectric material, it contains

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Quartz is a well-known crystalline allotropic form of silica (silicon dioxide, \(\mathrm{SiO}_2\)). It exhibits the piezoelectric effect, producing an electric potential when mechanical stress is applied, and is therefore widely utilized in quartz clocks and electronic oscillators.

Step 2: Composition Evaluation
Silicon dioxide consists of silicon and oxygen atoms arranged in a continuous three-dimensional network of corner-sharing \(\mathrm{SiO}_4\) tetrahedra. Therefore, quartz contains the element silicon (\(\mathrm{Si}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Quartz contains the element silicon (\(\mathrm{Si}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q13 - Identification of commonly used reducing agent

questiontext.text: The most commonly used reducing agent is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Group 14 elements, the stability of the \(+4\) oxidation state decreases down the group while the stability of the \(+2\) oxidation state increases due to the inert pair effect. For tin (\(\mathrm{Sn}\)), the \(+4\) oxidation state is more stable than the \(+2\) oxidation state.

Step 2: Redox Behavior of Tin(II) Chloride
Because \(\mathrm{Sn}^{4+}\) is more stable than \(\mathrm{Sn}^{2+}\), tin(II) species readily lose two electrons to become oxidised to tin(IV):
\[\mathrm{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Sn}^{4+} + 2e^{-}\]
By donating electrons and causing the reduction of other substances, \(\mathrm{SnCl}_2\) functions as a widely used laboratory reducing agent. In contrast, lead(II) is stable and does not act as a reducing agent, tin in \(\mathrm{SnCl}_4\) is already in its maximum oxidation state, and \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) is a non-redox Lewis acid.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The most commonly used reducing agent is tin(II) chloride (\(\mathrm{SnCl}_2\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q14 - Chemical identity of common dry ice

questiontext.text: Dry ice is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dry ice is the common name given to carbon dioxide in its solid form. At standard atmospheric pressure, solid carbon dioxide sublimes directly to the gaseous state at \(-78.5\text{ }^\circ\text{C}\) (\(194.65\text{ K}\)) without passing through an intermediate liquid phase.

Step 2: Final Conclusion
Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q15 - Periodic groups of oxide components in cement

questiontext.text: Cement, the important building material is a mixture of oxides of several elements. Besides calcium, iron and sulphur, oxides of elements of which of the group (s) are present in the mixture?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Portland cement is manufactured by combining raw materials that yield a mixture of inorganic oxides. The major oxide components are calcium oxide (\(\mathrm{CaO}\), \(50\text{--}60\%\)), silica (\(\mathrm{SiO}_2\), \(20\text{--}25\%\)), alumina (\(\mathrm{Al}_2\mathrm{O}_3\), \(5\text{--}10\%\)), magnesium oxide (\(\mathrm{MgO}\), \(2\text{--}3\%\)), iron oxide (\(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3\), \(1\text{--}2\%\)), and sulphur trioxide (\(\mathrm{SO}_3\), \(1\text{--}2\%\)).

Step 2: Group Classification of Elements
Besides calcium (\(\mathrm{Ca}\), Group 2), iron (\(\mathrm{Fe}\), d-block), and sulphur (\(\mathrm{S}\), Group 16), the remaining elements whose oxides are present are:
- Magnesium (\(\mathrm{Mg}\)) in Group 2
- Aluminium (\(\mathrm{Al}\)) in Group 13
- Silicon (\(\mathrm{Si}\)) in Group 14

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Oxides of elements belonging to groups 2, 13, and 14 are present in the cement mixture.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q16 - Reasons for smaller atomic radius of gallium

questiontext.text: The reason for small radius of Ga compared to Al is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Atomic radius generally increases down a group due to the addition of successive principal energy shells. However, gallium (\(135\text{ pm}\)) has a slightly smaller atomic radius than aluminium (\(143\text{ pm}\)) due to poor shielding by intervening inner subshell electrons.

Step 2: Electronic Configuration and Screening Evaluation
The electronic configuration of gallium is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\, 3d^{10}\, 4s^2\, 4p^1\), whereas aluminium is \([\mathrm{Ne}]\, 3s^2\, 3p^1\). Gallium has ten intervening \(3d\)-electrons. The \(d\)-orbitals are diffuse in shape and exert a poor screening (shielding) effect. Consequently, the increased nuclear charge (from \(Z = 13\) in aluminium to \(Z = 31\) in gallium) is not effectively shielded, causing the valence electrons to experience a greater effective nuclear attraction and pulling the electron cloud closer to the nucleus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The small radius of gallium compared to aluminium is due to the poor screening effect of the \(d\) and \(f\) orbitals and the increase in nuclear charge.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q17 - Hybridisation and bonding underlying linear carbon dioxide

questiontext.text: The linear shape of \(\mathrm{CO}_{2}\) is due to

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The geometry of a covalent molecule is determined by the hybridisation state of the central atom and the arrangement of its \(\sigma\) bonds and lone pairs to minimize electron-pair repulsions.

Step 2: Bonding in Carbon Dioxide
In \(\mathrm{CO}_2\), the central carbon atom forms two \(\sigma\) bonds and two \(\pi\) bonds with the two oxygen atoms (\(\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\)). To form two collinear \(\sigma\) bonds, the central carbon atom utilizes \(sp\) hybrid orbitals oriented at \(180^\circ\) to each other. The two unhybridised \(2p\) orbitals of carbon overlap laterally with corresponding \(2p\) orbitals of the oxygen atoms to form two mutually perpendicular \(p\pi-p\pi\) double bonds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The linear shape of carbon dioxide is due to the \(sp\) hybridisation of the carbon atom and \(p\pi-p\pi\) bonding between carbon and oxygen.

answer.text: \(p\pi - p\pi\) bonding between carbon and oxygen

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q18 - Function of trimethylchlorosilane in silicone polymerisation process

questiontext.text: \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) is used during polymerisation of organo silicones because

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Polymerisation of silicones proceeds via the condensation of silanols formed by hydrolysis of chlorosilanes. Dichlorosilanes (\(\mathrm{Me}_2\mathrm{SiCl}_2\)) produce linear bifunctional units capable of continuous chain extension at both ends.

Step 2: End-Capping Mechanism
Monochlorosilane (\(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\)) hydrolyses to give monofunctional trimethylsilanol, \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiOH}\). Because it contains only one reactive hydroxyl group, it can react with only one growing end of a siloxane chain. Once attached, it leaves no remaining reactive sites at that terminal, effectively capping and blocking the chain end. By adjusting the concentration of \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\), the average chain length of the organo silicone polymer is directly controlled.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) is used because it controls the chain length of organo silicone polymers and blocks the terminal ends of the silicone polymer chain.

answer.text: the chain length of organo silicone polymers can be controlled by adding \(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\)
\(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) blocks the end terminal of silicone polymer
\(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) improves the quality and yield of the polymer
\(\mathrm{Me}_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) acts as a catalyst during polymerisation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q19 - True statements regarding fullerenes and graphite allotropes

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Fullerene Properties
Fullerenes (such as \(\mathrm{C}_{60}\)) consist of closed, hollow spherical or ellipsoidal cage-like molecules containing fused six-membered and five-membered carbon rings. Because all carbon valencies are fully satisfied within the closed cage, fullerenes do not have open surfaces or dangling bonds, making them pure discrete molecular forms of carbon.

Step 2: Evaluation of Graphite Properties
Graphite has a standard enthalpy of formation defined as zero (\(\Delta_{\mathrm{f}}H^\circ = 0\)), making it thermodynamically the most stable allotrope of carbon at standard conditions. In graphite, carbon atoms form two-dimensional planar hexagonal sheets held together by weak van der Waals forces, which makes graphite soft and slippery (not hard); hence, it is used as a dry lubricant in machinery.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that fullerenes are cage-like molecules and graphite is the thermodynamically most stable allotrope of carbon.

answer.text: Graphite is thermodynamically most stable allotrope of carbon
Graphite is slippery and hard and therefore used as a dry lubricant in machines

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q20 - Analysis of bonding and geometry in diborane

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct. Answer on the basis of Fig. 11.1.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analysis of Diborane Structure
In diborane (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)), each boron atom is \(sp^3\) hybridised. The molecule contains four terminal hydrogen atoms and two bridging hydrogen atoms linking the two boron atoms.

Step 2: Planarity and Geometry Consideration
The two boron atoms and the four terminal hydrogen atoms lie in one plane. The two bridging hydrogen atoms lie in a plane perpendicular to this plane, with one above and one below. Therefore, in their own perpendicular plane, the two bridged hydrogen atoms and the two boron atoms lie in one plane.

Step 3: Bond Classification
The four terminal \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are conventional two-centre two-electron (\(2c-2e\)) covalent \(\sigma\) bonds. The two bridging \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{B}\) bonds are three-centre two-electron (\(3c-2e\)) banana bonds, where each bridge shares one pair of electrons across three nuclei. Therefore, two of the six \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are \(3c-2e\) bonds, and the four terminal bonds are regular \(2c-2e\) bonds.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are: the two bridged hydrogen atoms and the two boron atoms lie in one plane; two of the six \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are three-centre two-electron bonds; and the four terminal \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are regular two-centre two-electron bonds.

answer.text: The two birdged hydrogen atoms and the two boron atoms lie in one plane;
Out of six B-H bonds two bonds can be described in terms of 3 centre 2-electron bonds.
Out of six B-H bonds four B-H bonds can be described in terms of 3 centre 2 electron bonds;
The four terminal B-H bonds are two centre-two electron regular bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q21 - Identification of valid resonance structures of carbon dioxide

questiontext.text: Identify the correct resonance structures of carbon dioxide from the ones given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Resonance structures of a molecule must be valid Lewis structures with the same overall charge, identical atomic positions, and an octet of electrons around second-period atoms (carbon and oxygen) wherever possible, with formal charges corresponding correctly to electron accounting.

Step 2: Evaluation of Structures
Carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO}_2\)) has a total of 16 valence electrons. The uncharged canonical structure is the symmetrical double-bonded form \(\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\), where each atom satisfies the octet rule with zero formal charges.
When a \(\pi\)-electron pair shifts toward one oxygen atom, that oxygen acquires a single bond and a formal charge of \(-1\), while the other oxygen forms a triple bond to carbon with a formal charge of \(+1\), yielding the dipolar contributing structure \({}^{-}\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{C}\equiv \mathrm{O}^{+}\) (and its equivalent mirror image \({}^{+}\mathrm{O}\equiv \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{O}^{-}\)). Both atoms maintain completed octets.
Structures lacking formal charges on single/triple bonds or showing an impossible triple bond to an anion with negative formal charge while having a positively charged single-bonded oxygen do not represent correct electronic distributions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct resonance structures of carbon dioxide are \(\mathrm{O}=\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\) and \({}^{-}\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{C}\equiv \mathrm{O}^{+}\).
